2. STEP 1 — INDEPENDENT DESIGN CLASSIFICATION & TOOL SELECTION (`RISK_OF_BIAS.md` §1):
   Classify the study's actual design from its Methods section, then select the matching appraisal tool:
   - `"RoB 2 (parallel-trial variant)"`: Individually randomized controlled trial. Rate all 5 domains (`D1` Randomization process; `D2` Deviations from intended interventions; `D3` Missing outcome data; `D4` Measurement of the outcome; `D5` Selection of the reported result) as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`, and overall rating as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`.
   - `"RoB 2 (cluster-randomized trials variant)"`: Cluster-randomized trial (villages, compounds, neighbourhoods, schools, utilities randomized as clusters). Rate all 6 domains (`D1a` Randomization process; `D1b` Timing of identification or recruitment of participants within clusters; `D2` Deviations from intended interventions; `D3` Missing outcome data; `D4` Measurement of the outcome; `D5` Selection of the reported result) as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`, and overall rating as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`.
   - `"ROBINS-I"`: Non-randomized study of an intervention / policy with a genuine comparator (DiD, IV, RDD, PSM, ITS, controlled before-after, comparative longitudinal/panel evaluation). Rate all 7 domains (`D1` Bias due to confounding; `D2` Bias in selection of participants into the study; `D3` Bias in classification of interventions; `D4` Bias due to deviations from intended interventions; `D5` Bias due to missing data; `D6` Bias in measurement of outcomes; `D7` Bias in selection of the reported result — note `No information` honestly if no pre-analysis plan/protocol exists) as `"Low"`, `"Moderate"`, `"Serious"`, `"Critical"`, or `"No information"`, and overall rating in the same vocabulary. Do NOT assign single-case histories with no comparator arm to ROBINS-I!
   - `"JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies"`: Quantitative cross-sectional survey / observational regression without a quasi-experimental intervention structure. Rate all 8 items (`Q1` Inclusion criteria in sample clearly defined; `Q2` Study subjects and setting described in detail; `Q3` Exposure measured validly and reliably; `Q4` Objective, standard criteria used for measurement of condition; `Q5` Confounding factors identified; `Q6` Strategies to deal with confounding factors stated; `Q7` Outcomes measured validly and reliably; `Q8` Appropriate statistical analysis used) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, `"Unclear"`, or `"Not applicable"`. Provide overall narrative judgment (`"Low concern"`, `"Some concern"`, or `"High concern"` — no numeric score).
   - `"JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Cohort Studies"`: Observational comparative cohort design (not framed as a ROBINS-I intervention). Rate all 11 items (`Q1` Similar groups from same population; `Q2` Exposures measured similarly; `Q3` Exposure measured validly/reliably; `Q4` Confounding factors identified; `Q5` Strategies to deal with confounding stated; `Q6` Participants free of outcome at start; `Q7` Outcomes measured validly/reliably; `Q8` Follow-up time reported and sufficient; `Q9` Follow-up complete or loss explored; `Q10` Strategies to address incomplete follow-up utilized; `Q11` Appropriate statistical analysis used) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, `"Unclear"`, or `"Not applicable"`, plus narrative overall judgment (`"Low concern"`, `"Some concern"`, `"High concern"`).
   - `"CASP Qualitative Checklist"`: Primary qualitative study (interviews, ethnography, focus groups, qualitative documentary/field case study). Rate all 10 items (`Q1` Clear statement of aims; `Q2` Qualitative methodology appropriate; `Q3` Research design appropriate to address aims; `Q4` Recruitment strategy appropriate to aims; `Q5` Data collected in a way that addressed research issue; `Q6` Relationship between researcher and participants adequately considered [reflexivity]; `Q7` Ethical issues considered; `Q8` Data analysis sufficiently rigorous; `Q9` Clear statement of findings; `Q10` How valuable is the research [narrative assessment]). Rate Q1-Q9 `"Yes"`, `"No"`, or `"Can't tell"`, and Q10 narratively; give narrative `overall_rating` (e.g. `"Low methodological concern"`, `"Moderate concern (X Can't tell / No items)"`, `"High methodological concern"` — no numeric score).
   - `"MMAT (Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool)"`: Genuine mixed-methods primary study combining qualitative AND quantitative empirical components (do NOT assign purely quantitative or purely qualitative studies to MMAT). Rate Screening `S1`-`S2`, Qualitative `1.1`-`1.5`, the matching Quantitative 5-item block (`2.1`-`2.5` randomized, `3.1`-`3.5` non-randomized, or `4.1`-`4.5` descriptive), AND Mixed-Methods integration `5.1`-`5.5` (`5.1` adequate rationale for mixed methods; `5.2` components effectively integrated; `5.3` outputs of integration adequately interpreted; `5.4` divergences/inconsistencies adequately addressed; `5.5` components adhere to quality criteria of each tradition) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, or `"Can't tell"`. Per MMAT 2018 rules, NEVER compute a numeric score; provide a concise criterion-grounded narrative `overall_rating` noting that overall quality cannot exceed the weakest component.
   - `"AMSTAR 2"`: Secondary systematic review, meta-analysis, or scoping review with an explicit systematic search/screening method (NEVER apply AMSTAR 2 to non-systematic narrative literature reviews!). Rate all 16 items `Q1`-`Q16` (explicitly marking critical domains `Q2`, `Q4`, `Q7`, `Q9`, `Q11`, `Q13`, `Q15`) as `"Yes"`, `"Partial Yes"` (where applicable), `"No"`, or `"Not applicable (no meta-analysis)"`, and apply AMSTAR 2 overall confidence (`"High"`, `"Moderate"`, `"Low"`, `"Critically Low"`).
   - `"Legal Institutional Evidence Appraisal Framework"`: Doctrinal-empirical hybrid, jurimetric analysis, or institutional/legal-historical case study that fits NONE of the six conventional designs above. Rate all 13 narrative domains (`D1` Legal source accuracy; `D2` Jurisdictional specificity; `D3` Exposure definition; `D4` Outcome definition; `D5` Sampling transparency; `D6` Selection process; `D7` Measurement transparency; `D8` Causal identification; `D9` Treatment of confounding; `D10` Institutional context; `D11` Replication potential; `D12` Coding transparency; `D13` Researcher reflexivity) as `"strong"`, `"adequate"`, `"weak"`, or `"not assessable"`. Explicitly frame `overall_rating` as a structured non-validated judgment (NEVER a numeric composite score!).
   - `"NONE"`: Use when the study fits NONE of the listed instruments (e.g., pure mathematical/simulation optimization model with no empirical sample, or non-systematic narrative essay/review with no primary empirical method and no systematic search). Set `overall_rating = "NOT APPLICABLE (design fits no listed tool)"`, explain clearly in `why_tool_chosen` and `overall_narrative_summary` rather than forcing an inappropriate checklist, and still fill the 7 `cross_tool_domains` honestly from the paper!

cross_tool_domains.attrition: Low risk for primary administrative payment outcomes (0% missing data across all 2,584 compounds in the engagement trial and all 1,001 compounds in the enforcement ITT analysis via automated utility billing records). Some concerns for secondary 9-month follow-up survey outcomes in enforcement-treatment clusters (out of 649 eligible compounds: N=589-608 for compound water/sanitation indicators, N=474 [27% missing] for physical meter readings, N=334 [49% missing] for household monthly water expenditure, and N=357-403 for tenant survey outcomes), with no arm-specific survey attrition balance tests reported.
cross_tool_domains.confounding: Low risk. Both interventions used randomized assignment stratified by informal settlement (individual compound randomization for engagement; two-stage street-cluster randomization for contract enforcement). Multi-year pre-intervention administrative payment trajectories (2014 to October 2018, Figure 5) and 45 baseline balance tests (Table A3) confirm strong comparability across arms, and robustness regressions controlling for minor baseline imbalances (water connection status and presence of paying tenants, p<0.05) left treatment estimates unchanged.
cross_tool_domains.legal_measurement_quality: Strong. The contractual enforcement exposure is grounded in written utility upgrade contracts signed by property owners and Kenya's 2016 Water Act / WASREB regulatory framework, and is operationalized via explicit administrative arrears rules (>US$ 25 consumption balance plus missed monthly payments), standardized tablet scripts and posted 14-day disconnection notices with hardship appeal channels (Appendix B), and exact administrative tracking of notice delivery (299/327 = 91.4%), physical disconnections (96 compounds), and reconnections.
cross_tool_domains.measurement_bias: Low risk for primary revenue collection and loan repayment outcomes (measured objectively via the automated Jisomee Mita electronic utility billing platform) and for enumerator-verified compound connections and physical water meter readings. Some concerns for secondary survey outcomes at 9 months (self-reported monthly water expenditure, weekly water-fetching minutes, perceptions of utility fairness and quality, owner-tenant relationships, and rental income), as participants were unblinded to disconnection notices and survey enumerator blinding within treatment clusters is not reported.
cross_tool_domains.outcome_measurement_quality: Strong for utility financial outcomes (5 years of high-frequency electronic billing, invoice, consumption, and loan-repayment records) and adequate-to-strong for household water and sanitation outcomes, which combine direct enumerator observation of piped water and pour-flush sewer connections and on-site meter readings with noisy self-reported water expenditure and weekly fetching time (with no microbiological water quality testing and unanalyzed child health data).
cross_tool_domains.reporting_bias: Some concerns. The experiments were registered in the AEA RCT Registry (AEARCTR-0003556), primary payment analyses follow the specified ITT equations, and all individual sub-indicators underlying the Anderson (2008) summary indices are fully reported in Appendix Tables A1, A2, and A6. However, maternal-reported under-five child health outcomes were collected at endline and omitted from analysis post hoc (explicitly disclosed in Section 8.5), and the follow-up survey analyses (Tables 7-8) restrict the control group to within-cluster control compounds in enforcement-treatment clusters rather than the pure control clusters specified in Equation (2).
cross_tool_domains.selection_bias: Low risk for compound-level administrative outcomes (eligible accounts were enumerated from the utility database and August 2018 phone census prior to random assignment). Some concerns for endline tenant-level survey outcomes because one tenant per compound was randomly sampled 9 months post-intervention, after the enforcement treatment significantly increased the proportion of compounds renting out dwellings by 13.5 percentage points (from 58.9% to 72.4%, p<0.001), potentially altering the composition of surveyed tenants; additionally, two dense multi-story settlements were excluded from the enforcement trial for technical feasibility reasons (external validity limitation).

domain_ratings.justification: Randomization was performed centrally by the research team using administrative billing snapshots downloaded on 6 August 2018 (engagement trial: 2,584 compounds with tenants randomized 1:1 to 1,292 treatment and 1,292 control, stratified by settlement) and 28 October 2018 (enforcement trial: 3,253 accounts in 4 settlements grouped via GPS/address into 147 street clusters, with 73 clusters randomized to treatment and 74 to pure control, stratified by settlement, and 327 of 649 disconnection-eligible compounds within treatment clusters randomized to disconnection notices). Baseline balance across 45 comparisons (Table A3) and 4 years of pre-trend billing data (Figure 5) show strong balance; controlling for the slight imbalance in baseline tenant presence and water connection status did not alter estimates.

domain_ratings.justification: All 147 street clusters and all disconnection-eligible compounds/property owners were identified from the August/September 2018 listing census and October 2018 utility billing records prior to cluster and within-cluster random assignment, yielding low risk for all compound-level administrative outcomes. However, for the August-October 2019 endline tenant survey (Table 7), one tenant per compound was sampled 9 months post-intervention, and the enforcement intervention significantly increased the share of compounds renting out space by 13.5 percentage points (Table 8, p<0.001), introducing potential post-randomization recruitment/composition differences among surveyed tenants.

domain_ratings.justification: Participants and utility outreach/enforcement staff could not be blinded to face-to-face engagement visits or posted/SMS/phone disconnection notices. Delivery compliance was 69% (885/1,292) for engagement and 91.4% (299/327) for disconnection notices (with 28 compounds already disconnected prior to notice delivery), and control compounds were exempted from utility disconnections during the study period. The authors appropriately estimated Intention-to-Treat (ITT) effects for all randomized units and leveraged the two-stage cluster design to directly test within-street spillovers on untreated eligible and ineligible compounds, finding precise null spillover effects (Table 6).

raw_response.overall_narrative_summary: This study reports two sequential field experiments conducted with Nairobi's municipal water and sanitation utility (NCWSC) across informal settlements to improve service bill and last-mile connection loan repayment: (1) an individually randomized trial of face-to-face tenant engagement across 2,584 compounds with tenants, and (2) a two-stage street-level cluster-randomized controlled trial of transparent, credible service-contract disconnection notices across 147 street clusters (327 treated disconnection-eligible compounds, 322 within-cluster spillover controls, and 674 disconnection-eligible controls in 74 pure control clusters). Appraised using the RoB 2 cluster-randomized trial variant, the study has Low risk of bias for its primary payment and loan-repayment outcomes—which rely on centralized randomization, verified 4-year pre-intervention baseline balance, intention-to-treat estimation, explicit spillover testing, and 100% follow-up via automated Jisomee Mita utility billing records—and Some concerns overall when incorporating the 9-month endline owner and tenant survey outcomes (water/sanitation access, water expenditure, perceptions, well-being, and rental markets). Those concerns stem from sampling one tenant per compound at endline after treatment increased rental occupancy by 13.5 percentage points (D1b), unanalyzed item-level survey and meter-reading nonresponse (D3), unblinded respondent self-reports on secondary outcomes (D4), and the disclosed post-collection omission of under-five child health outcomes alongside restricting the endline survey sample to enforcement-treatment clusters rather than pure control clusters (D5).
raw_response.study_design_identified: Two sequential randomized field experiments: (1) a parallel compound-randomized controlled trial of face-to-face tenant outreach/engagement (N = 2,584 compounds with tenants across 6 settlements) and (2) a two-stage street-level cluster-randomized controlled trial of utility service-contract enforcement via credible disconnection notices (147 street clusters across 4 settlements; 327 treated eligible compounds, 322 within-cluster spillover controls, and 674 pure-cluster eligible controls).
raw_response.where_found_summary: Experimental design and sample flow in Section 4 (PDF pp. 12-14), Section 5 (PDF pp. 15-16), and Figures 3-4 (PDF p. 30); ITT and spillover estimators in Section 6 (PDF p. 16); administrative Jisomee Mita and survey outcome definitions in Section 7 (PDF pp. 16-18); baseline balance in Section 8.1 (PDF p. 18) and Table A3 (PDF p. 51); main treatment, spillover, water/sanitation, perception, and rental results in Sections 8.2-8.8 (PDF pp. 19-22) and Tables 4-8 (PDF pp. 35-38); IRB, AEA registry (AEARCTR-0003556), ethics, and intervention scripts/notices in Appendices A-B (PDF pp. 39-48).
raw_response.why_tool_chosen: Selected RoB 2 (cluster-randomized trials variant) because the study is a primary experimental evaluation whose focal legal/institutional intervention—contract enforcement of utility disconnection clauses, which is also the sole experiment followed up for water/sanitation access, welfare, and rental market outcomes—was randomized at the street-cluster level (147 street clusters in a two-stage cluster-randomized design, Section 5-6) across multi-household compounds. The cluster-RCT variant captures all standard parallel-trial RoB 2 domains (applicable to both the engagement and enforcement experiments) while additionally assessing D1b (timing of identification/recruitment of individual tenants within compounds/clusters), which directly applies to the endline tenant survey.
